latin.1659: I. Primum hominem, antequam peccaret, non fuisse morti obnoxium; quemadmodum jam sumus omnes, sed aliquo sensu immortalem, res est apud omnes Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae confessa. Nam communi consensu tuentur adversus Pelagianos necessitatem moriendi, quae jam nobis incumbit, ex peccato ortum habuisse; nec fuisse locum habituram, si homo in primaeva illa integritate permansisset.
latin.1660: II. Verum ut quae sit hac de re eorum sententia melius percipiatur, observant primum hominem in statu integritatis aliquo sensu mortalem, & aliquo sensu immortalem fuisse. Bifariam enim aliquis mortalis dici potest, ac totidem modis immortalis. Uno modo mortalis est quem necesse est mori. Altero modo mortalis dicitur qui potest mori. Et rursum uno modo immortalis est qui non potest mori. Altero modo quem non necesse est mori.
latin.1661: III. Priori modo, ex eorum mente, Adam in primo statu non fuit mortalis, sed tantum posteriori. Siquidem eum mori necesse nihil erat: nec si in originali justitia perseverasset, revera fuisset mortuus. Sed tamen contingere poterat ut moreretur, quemadmodum revera post lapsum illius contigit. Per peccatum autem & ipse, & tota ejus posteritas facta est mortalis priori modo, quia necessitatem moriendi incurrit. Similiter homo in statu innocentiae priori modo non erat immortalis; nec enim erat talis qui simpliciter mori non posset. Verum immortalis erat posteriori modo, siquidem poterat non mori, & fidelis manens in Dei obsequio mortem expertus non fuisset.
latin.1662: IV. Unde colligi potest discrimen inter immortalitatem primi hominis in statu integritatis, & illam quae competet justis post beatam resurrectionem. Nam Sancti post resurrectionem nullo modo mortales erunt: nec enim solum immunes erunt a necessitate moriendi, sed prorsus mori non poterunt, & peccando mortem aut mortalitatem incurrere. Et ita immortales erunt utroque modo, quia non solum poterunt non mori, sed mori non poterunt, & mors non poterit unquam ullam in eos habere potestatem.
latin.1663: V. Hac in re tamen explicanda inter Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae notari potest quaedam diversitas. In hoc illi quidem conveniunt omnes Adamum in statu integro potuisse non mori, & revera ni peccasset nunquam fuisse moriturum. Sed inter se disputant An Adam integer manens dici tantum debeat potuisse non mori? Num vero etiam dici possit, illum in isto statu non potuisse mori?
latin.1664: VI. Nonnulli sunt qui dicunt hominem, etiam stante ejus innocentia, mori semper potuisse, & primi hominis immortalitatem in eo tantum consistere quod non esset necessitati moriendi subjectus, sicut jam per peccatum sumus. Hominem enim quamvis permanentem in integritate mori potuisse, si ferro, igne, vel alio quocunque modo vis ejus corpori allata fuisset ab alio qui innocentiam primam deseruisset: quamvis nihil tale fuisset eventurum, eo quod Deus per suam providentiam omne periculum avertisset.
latin.1665: VII. Quin addunt primum hominem, & omnes ejus posteros, naturae necessitate tandem morituros fuisse, nimirum propter elementorum pugnam, ex quibus compositum est corpus humanum, nisi Deus, antequam illud accideret, eos transtulisset ad statum immortalitatis, talemque mortem, si accidisset, non magis homini quam bestiis poenalem futuram fuisse, sed utrisque naturalem. Unde sequitur hominem, quanquam persistentem in integritate, semper habuisse moriendi potestatem; nec de eo vere dici quod in eo statu mori non posset: quamvis posset non mori, & non esset necessitati moriendi subjectus. Hanc sententiam Estius tribuit Scoto & quibusdam aliis. In lib. 2. sentent. distinct. 19. num. 2.
latin.1666: VIII. Ipse vero ibidem & numero sequenti testatur se, cum multis aliis, in diversa esse sententia. Nam omnino dicendum putat quod homo, stante prima innocentia, non potuit mori. Nec enim simpliciter futurum fuisse ut homo in obsequio Dei persistens non moreretur, sed etiam ordinem rerum a Deo semel institutum necessario istud exegisse, neque aliter potuisse fieri.
latin.1667: IX. Ad cujus rei intelligentiam monet hominem non esse a Deo institutum ut creaturam mere servilem, sicut instituta est brutorum natura, quae proinde naturaliter & morti sunt obnoxia, & pro utilitate hominum occidi possunt: imo & alia aliis per mortem in usum nutrimenti cedunt: sed Deum fecisse hominem, perinde ut angelos, natura sua liberum, & aliarum rerum Dominum, atque insuper ipsius Dei per gratiam & justitiam velut socium & amicum. Indeque satis intelligi sic hominem institutum esse, ut ei nihil adversum accideret, quamdiu in Dei amicitia permaneret: sed futurum ut semper juncta essent, seque invicem consequerentur haec duo: bonum esse & beatum esse: itemque innocentem esse & expertem esse miseriae. Et hanc legem ita esse perpetuam, sic justitia divina postulante, ut ea sublata ordo universi deformaretur.
latin.1668: X. Haec tamen intelligenda dicit juxta ordinem semel institutum. Nam, inquit, si de absoluta Dei potentia loquamur, non dubium quin ita potuerit humanam naturam, absque ulla ejus injuria, tanquam totius creaturae Dominus instituere, ut licet homo in anima conservaret innocentiam, corporis tamen conditione brutis animalibus similis esset, morti caeterisque non minus quam illa obnoxius. Itaque licet Adam in statu innocentiae peccare potuerit, & per peccatum morti fieri obnoxius, & sic verum sit in sensu diviso Adamum integrum potuisse mori, pertendit tamen idem falsum esse in sensu conjuncto, quia mori non poterat, quamdiu servaret innocentiam.
latin.1669: XI. Verum utcunque istam primi hominis immortalitatem explicent Scholae Romanae Theologi, in eo videntur jam omnes convenire illam dici debere supernaturalem, non vero naturalem, prout scilicet, naturale opponitur supernaturali. Id praesertim affirmat & multis argumentis probare conatur Bellarminus. lib. de Gratia primi hominis cap. 9. Et Becanus in summa Theologiae Scholasticae. tom. 1. tract. 5. cap. 4. quaest. 1.
latin.1670: XII. Fuerunt quidem nonnulli superiore saeculo, inter ipsos Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, qui existimaverunt immortalitatem primi hominis non fuisse gratiae beneficium, sed naturalem ejus conditionem. Verum haec sententia fuit a Pontificibus Romanis Pio V. & Gregorio XIII. damnata in bulla singulari, in qua multos articulos recentiorum quorundam Theologorum damnaverunt. Inter quos articulos hic est 75. Immortalitas primi hominis non erat gratiae beneficium, sed naturalis ejus conditio. Ut testatur idem Bellarm. lib. de Grat. primi hominis.

sections.title: All Roman doctors confess that the first man was not liable to death before sin
sections.pass_a: That the first man, before he sinned, was not liable to death, as we all now are, but in some sense immortal, is a thing confessed among all the Doctors of the Roman Church. For by common consent they maintain against the Pelagians that the necessity of dying, which now lies upon us, had its origin from sin; and that it would have had no place, if man had remained in that primeval integrity.
pass_b: All the teachers of the Roman Church admit that the first man, before he sinned, was not subject to death as we all now are, but was in some sense immortal.
Against the Pelagians they hold by common consent that the necessity of dying which now lies on us arose from sin, and would have had no place if man had remained in his original integrity.

choices.why: The qualifier sets up the distinctions of the next theses; the English keeps it hedged.

sections.title: Two senses of mortal and immortal: must die or can die; cannot die or need not die
sections.pass_a: But so that what their opinion on this matter is may be better perceived, they observe that the first man in the state of integrity was in some sense mortal, and in some sense immortal. For someone can be called mortal in two ways, and immortal in as many ways. In one way he is mortal who must die. In the other way he is called mortal who can die. And again in one way he is immortal who cannot die. In the other way he whom it is not necessary to die.
pass_b: To make their view on this clearer, they point out that in the state of integrity the first man was mortal in one sense and immortal in another.

A person can be called mortal in two ways, and immortal in two ways. In the first way, a mortal is one who must die; in the second, one who can die. Likewise, in the first way an immortal is one who cannot die; in the second, one who does not have to die.

choices.english: one who does not have to die
choices.why: Keeps the contrast between necessity and possibility that the whole thesis turns on.
rejected: one who need not be dead

sections.title: Adam was mortal only as able to die, and immortal only as able not to die
sections.pass_a: In the former way, in their mind, Adam in the first state was not mortal, but only in the latter. Since it was in no way necessary that he die: nor, if he had persevered in original justice, would he in fact have died. But yet it could happen that he died, as in fact happened after his fall. But through sin both he himself and all his posterity were made mortal in the former way, because he incurred the necessity of dying. Likewise man in the state of innocence was not immortal in the former way; for he was not such that he simply could not die. But he was immortal in the latter way, since he was able not to die, and remaining faithful in obedience to God he would not have experienced death.
pass_b: In their view Adam in his first state was not mortal in the first sense, only in the second. There was no necessity at all that he die, and had he persevered in original righteousness he would never actually have died. Yet it was possible for him to die, as in fact happened after his fall. Through sin he and all his descendants became mortal in the first sense, because he brought on himself the necessity of dying.

In the same way, man in the state of innocence was not immortal in the first sense, for he was not such that he simply could not die. He was immortal in the second sense: he was able not to die, and had he stayed faithful in obeying God he would never have tasted death.

lemmas.gloss: brought on himself the necessity of dying

choices.english: he was able not to die
choices.why: The Augustinian posse non mori; the English keeps the order of 'able' and 'not'.

sections.title: The risen saints will be immortal in both senses, unlike Adam in innocence
sections.pass_a: Whence can be gathered the difference between the immortality of the first man in the state of integrity, and that which will belong to the just after the blessed resurrection. For the Saints after the resurrection will in no way be mortal: for not only will they be immune from the necessity of dying, but they will be wholly unable to die, and by sinning to incur death or mortality. And so they will be immortal in both ways, because not only will they be able not to die, but they will not be able to die, and death will never be able to have any power over them.
pass_b: From this one can see how the first man's immortality in the state of integrity differs from the immortality the just will have after the blessed resurrection.

After the resurrection the saints will not be mortal in any way. They will not only be free from the necessity of dying; they will be altogether unable to die, or to bring death or mortality on themselves by sinning. So they will be immortal in both senses: they will not only be able not to die, they will be unable to die, and death will never have any power over them.

lemmas.gloss: free from the necessity of dying

choices.english: they will be unable to die
choices.why: The non posse mori of the blessed, set against Adam's posse non mori.

notes: The final clause echoes Romans 6:9 ('death hath no more dominion over him'), said there of the risen Christ; the print gives no reference.

sections.title: Rome's doctors agree Adam could avoid death, but dispute whether he could not die
sections.pass_a: Yet in explaining this matter a certain diversity can be noted among the Doctors of the Roman Church. In this indeed they all agree, that Adam in the integral state was able not to die, and in fact had he not sinned would never have died. But they dispute among themselves Whether Adam, remaining integral, ought to be said only to have been able not to die? Or whether it can also be said that in that state he was not able to die?
pass_b: In explaining this, however, the teachers of the Roman Church differ somewhat among themselves. They all agree that Adam in his unfallen state was able not to die, and that had he not sinned he would in fact never have died.
But they dispute whether we should say only that Adam, while he remained upright, was able not to die, or whether we may also say that in that state he was unable to die.

choices.why: Le Blanc frames the dispute as posse non mori versus non posse mori; the English keeps the two formulas distinct.

sections.title: Some say unfallen man could always die by violence, though providence would have prevented it
sections.pass_a: There are some who say that man, even while his innocence stood, could always have died, and that the immortality of the first man consisted only in this, that he was not subject to the necessity of dying, as we now are through sin. For man, although remaining in integrity, could have died, if by iron, fire, or in any other way whatever violence had been brought to his body by another who had abandoned the first innocence: although nothing such would have happened, because God by his providence would have averted every danger.
pass_b: Some say that man could always have died, even while his innocence stood, and that the first man's immortality consisted only in his not being subject to the necessity of dying, as we now are through sin.

For although man remained in integrity, they say, he could have died if someone who had abandoned the first innocence had done violence to his body by sword, by fire, or in any other way at all. Nothing of the kind would actually have happened, since God by his providence would have turned every danger aside.

choices.english: Nothing of the kind would actually have happened
choices.why: The concession is part of the opinion reported; the English marks it as their own qualification.

sections.title: They add that elemental strife would at last have killed unfallen man, unless God translated him (Scotus)
sections.pass_a: Nay, they add that the first man and all his posterity would at last have died by necessity of nature, namely on account of the conflict of the elements of which the human body is composed, unless God, before that happened, had translated them to a state of immortality, and that such a death, if it had happened, would have been no more penal for man than for beasts, but natural for both. Whence it follows that man, although persisting in integrity, always had the power of dying; nor could it truly be said of him that in that state he could not die: although he was able not to die, and was not subject to the necessity of dying. This opinion Estius attributes to Scotus and certain others. On book 2 of the Sentences, distinction 19, number 2.
pass_b: They even add that the first man and all his descendants would in the end have died by a necessity of nature, because of the conflict of the elements that make up the human body, unless God had carried them over into a state of immortality before that happened. Such a death, had it occurred, would have been no more a punishment for man than for the beasts; for both it would have been natural.

It follows that man, even persisting in integrity, always had the capacity to die. It could not truly be said of him that in that state he was unable to die, although he was able not to die and was not subject to the necessity of dying.
Estius attributes this view to Scotus and certain others (Estius on the Sentences, book 2, distinction 19, number 2).

choices.english: although he was able not to die
choices.why: Le Blanc's 'posset non mori' is the possibility of not dying, not 'could not die'.

notes: Estius is Willem Hessels van Est, commentator on Peter Lombard's Sentences.

sections.title: Estius himself holds that unfallen man could not die, by the order God established
sections.pass_a: But he himself in the same place and in the following number testifies that he, with many others, is of a different opinion. For he thinks it must altogether be said that man, while the first innocence stood, could not die. For it was not simply going to be that man persisting in obedience to God would not die, but also that the order of things once instituted by God necessarily required this, and it could not have happened otherwise.
pass_b: Estius himself, in the same place and in the next number, declares that he and many others hold a different view. He thinks we must say outright that while his first innocence stood man was unable to die.
It was not merely that man, persisting in obedience to God, would in fact not have died. The order of things God had once established necessarily required it, and it could not have been otherwise.

lemmas.latin: ordinem rerum a Deo semel institutum
lemmas.gloss: the order of things God had once established

choices.why: This is the stronger non posse mori, set against the posse non mori of the opinion before.

sections.title: Estius: man was made free, lord of things and God's friend, so no harm could befall him in God's friendship
sections.pass_a: For understanding which matter he warns that man was not instituted by God as a merely servile creature, as the nature of brutes was instituted, which therefore are naturally also liable to death, and can be killed for the utility of men: nay, and some yield to others through death for the use of nourishment: but that God made man, just like the angels, free by his nature, and lord of other things, and moreover through grace and justice as it were the companion and friend of God himself. And hence it is sufficiently understood that man was so instituted, that nothing adverse would befall him, as long as he remained in God's friendship: but that it would be that these two would always be joined, and would follow each other: to be good and to be blessed: and likewise to be innocent and to be free of misery. And that this law is so perpetual, divine justice so demanding, that if it were taken away the order of the universe would be deformed.
pass_b: To explain this, he points out that God did not make man a merely servile creature, as he made the nature of the brutes. They are therefore naturally subject to death and may be killed for men's use; indeed, some of them give way to others by death to serve as food. God made man, like the angels, free by nature and lord of other things, and besides that, through grace and righteousness, a kind of companion and friend of God himself.

From this, he says, it is clear enough that man was so made that nothing hostile would befall him as long as he remained in God's friendship. Two pairs would always go together and follow from each other: being good and being happy, and likewise being innocent and being free of misery.
And this law is so permanent, because divine justice requires it, that if it were removed the order of the universe would be disfigured.

choices.english: a kind of companion and friend
choices.why: Velut softens the claim; 'a kind of' keeps that hedge.

sections.title: By absolute power God could have made man mortal in body; Adam could die in the divided sense, not the composite
sections.pass_a: Yet he says these things are to be understood according to the order once instituted. For, he says, if we speak of the absolute power of God, there is no doubt that he could, as Lord of the whole creation, have so instituted human nature, without any injury to it, that although man kept innocence in his soul, yet in the condition of his body he would be like the brute animals, liable no less than they to death and other things. Therefore although Adam in the state of innocence could sin, and through sin become liable to death, and so it is true in the divided sense that Adam integral could die, he nevertheless maintains that the same is false in the composite sense, because he could not die as long as he kept his innocence.
pass_b: He says, however, that all this must be understood of the order God once established. "If we speak of God's absolute power," he says, "there is no doubt that as Lord of all creation he could, without wronging it, have so made human nature that, although man kept his innocence in his soul, in the condition of his body he would have been like the brute animals, subject to death and the rest no less than they are."

So, although Adam in the state of innocence could sin and through sin become subject to death, and in that sense (the divided sense) it is true that unfallen Adam could die, Estius insists that the same statement is false in the composite sense, because he could not die as long as he kept his innocence.

choices.why: Ejus refers to human nature; the point is that God would do it no injustice.

sections.title: However they explain it, Rome's theologians now agree the first man's immortality was supernatural
sections.pass_a: But however the Theologians of the Roman School explain that immortality of the first man, in this all now seem to agree, that it ought to be called supernatural, not natural, namely as natural is opposed to supernatural. This especially Bellarmine affirms and tries to prove with many arguments. Book on the Grace of the first man, chapter 9. And Becanus in the summa of Scholastic Theology, tome 1, treatise 5, chapter 4, question 1.
pass_b: However the theologians of the Roman school explain this immortality of the first man, they all now seem to agree on one point: it must be called supernatural, not natural, in the sense in which natural is opposed to supernatural.

Bellarmine above all affirms this and tries to prove it with many arguments (On the Grace of the First Man, chapter 9), as does Becanus (Summa of Scholastic Theology, tome 1, treatise 5, chapter 4, question 1).

lemmas.gloss: in the sense in which natural is opposed to supernatural

choices.why: The technical pair is kept; Le Blanc will distinguish senses of 'natural' in what follows.

notes: Becanus is the Jesuit Martin Becanus (d. 1624), Summa theologiae scholasticae.

sections.title: The contrary view, that immortality was man's natural condition, was condemned by Pius V and Gregory XIII
sections.pass_a: There were indeed some in the former century, among the Doctors of the Roman Church themselves, who thought that the immortality of the first man was not a benefit of grace, but his natural condition. But this opinion was condemned by the Roman Pontiffs Pius V and Gregory XIII in a particular bull, in which they condemned many articles of certain more recent Theologians. Among which articles this is the 75th. The immortality of the first man was not a benefit of grace, but his natural condition. As the same Bellarmine testifies, book on the Grace of the first man.
pass_b: In the last century there were indeed some among the teachers of the Roman Church itself who held that the first man's immortality was not a gift of grace but his natural condition.

But the Roman popes Pius V and Gregory XIII condemned this view in a special bull in which they condemned many articles of certain recent theologians. Article 75 among them reads: "The immortality of the first man was not a gift of grace, but his natural condition." So Bellarmine himself testifies (On the Grace of the First Man).

choices.why: Singularis here means a particular, separate bull, not an extraordinary one.

notes: The bull is Pius V's condemnation of propositions of Michael Baius (Ex omnibus afflictionibus, 1567), renewed by Gregory XIII (1579). Le Blanc numbers the article 75 after Bellarmine; later collections number it differently.
